newsitem.title: FRANCE: Basque leader says ETA willing to talk to Madrid.
newsitem.headline: Basque leader says ETA willing to talk to Madrid.

text.p: Spanish Basque nationalist leader Xabier Arzallus believes ETA guerrillas want to open talks with the Madrid government on ending their three-decade-old violent campaign for a separate Basque state.

Arzallus said in an interview published on Friday by the French daily Le Monde he could not vouch for ETA's (Basque Homeland and Freedom) will to negotiate since the group had twice in the past broken off talks.
"But this time I believe they want to do it," he added.
He recalled that ETA had proposed a basis for discussion in 1995 and was now finding it hard to cope, as some 600 of its members were in Spanish prisons and 2,000 in exile.
"This is hard to cope with, and many believe the current struggle has no future," he said.

The conservative Spanish government has rejected talks with the separatists unless they end violence, and Arzallus blamed rightist hardliners close to Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar for Madrid's stance.

"I believe he has people around him who would make your (far-rightist politician Jean-Marie) Le Pen look like a democrat, and for whom it would be humiliating for the state to be unable to settle the problem otherwise than through police force," he said.

Arzallus, president of the Basque region's leading political force, the moderate Basque Nationalist Party (PNV), reminded Aznar that the conditions for PNV support for the minority Madrid government were that it help complete devolution of power to the Basque regional government.
"If (Aznar) does not abide by the rules of the game, we'll drop him. And I am not sure that it would be in his interest," he said.

He said there were currently no contacts between Madrid and the guerrillas. Discussing the right to self-determination of the Basque country, one of the demands of ETA and the nationalists, would be a good basis for opening talks.
The conflict between Madrid and ETA has worsened as ETA guerrillas have stepped up their lethal attacks since the beginning of this year, killing six people including a Supreme Court judge.

Eighteen of the 25-member leadership of Herri Batasuna (HB), the ETA's political arm, have been arrested in the past few weeks for failing to answer a Spanish Supreme Court summons to appear on charges of distributing an illegal pro-ETA video during Spain's 1996 election campaign.

HB, which has an estimated 10 to 15 percent support in the Basque country, called a general strike in the region on Friday to protest against the arrests. The strike, outlawed by the regional government, failed to bite early in the day but there were scattered incidents throughout the region.
